references.text: Jesus also knew the Pharisees' thoughts when they wondered if he would heal on the Sabbath. Jesus' ability to see through people's inner motives and thoughts is a recurring theme in the Gospel of Luke ([ref:Luk 6:8|Luke 6:8]).
Jesus knew the thoughts of those who accused him of casting out demons by Beelzebul. This shows his divine insight into human hearts ([ref:Luk 11:17|Luke 11:17]).

Matthew's parallel account of the same event, where Jesus sees through the wickedness of the Pharisees and Herodians as they try to trap him with the question about paying taxes to Caesar ([ref:Matt 22:18|Matthew 22:18]).
Mark's parallel account where Jesus knows the hypocrisy of those who ask the question about paying taxes to Caesar ([ref:Mark 12:15|Mark 12:15]).

John emphasizes that Jesus knew all people and what was in a person, without anyone needing to testify about it. This is the theological background for why Jesus could see through panourgia (deceit) among his opponents ([ref:Joh 2:24-25|John 2:24-25]).

Paul quotes from Job and uses the same Greek word πανουργία (cunning/slyness) about human wisdom that God catches the wise in. This connects to how Jesus saw through his opponents' πανουργίαν (deceit) ([ref:1 Kor 3:19|1 Corinthians 3:19]).

The Lord knows people's thoughts. This psalm emphasizes God's omniscience about human inner life, which is reflected in Jesus' ability to see through his opponents' deceitful intentions ([ref:Sal 94:11|Psalm 94:11]).

The Lord searches the heart and tests the kidneys. Jeremiah's statement about God's insight into people's inner motives forms the background for Jesus seeing through his opponents' deceit ([ref:Jer 17:10|Jeremiah 17:10]).

God's word judges the thoughts and intentions of the heart, and no creature is hidden from him. This text reflects the divine omniscience that Jesus demonstrates when he sees through his opponents' deceit ([ref:Hebr 4:12-13|Hebrews 4:12-13]).
